passages.text: A Natural Enzyme GOx-MOF Cascade Complex Killing Zoonotic Parasite <italic>Trichinella spiralis</italic> by Energy Utilization Limitation and Generated Free Radicals

Nanozymes offer promising alternatives to natural enzymes due to enhanced stability, tunable activity, and cost efficiency, demonstrating therapeutic potential against tumors, infections, and inflammatory disorders. <sentence_start/><italic>Trichinella spiralis</italic> is an important pathogen, which globally prevalent foodborne zoonotic parasite. <sentence_start/>Chemical drug is commonly used to kill <italic>T. spiralis</italic>, but there are risks of chemical abuse and drug resistance. <sentence_start/>Here, we engineered MPG(Fe), a cascade nanozyme formed by covalently conjugating glucose oxidase (GOx) to a metal-organic framework-Fe nanozyme (MOF-525[Fe]) nanozyme via the bifunctional PEG linker. <sentence_start/>In vitro, MPG(Fe) depleted glucose through GOx-catalyzed conversion to gluconic acid and H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, while MOF-525(Fe) subsequently transformed H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> into cytotoxic hydroxyl radicals (•OH). <sentence_start/>This dual-action mechanism dose-dependently killed intestinal-stage adult worms and newborn larvae (NBL) of <italic>T. spiralis</italic>. <sentence_start/>In a BALB/c mouse model of intestinal <italic>T. spiralis</italic> infection, high-dose MPG(Fe) reduced the survival of intestinal adult worms to 3.53% of the control value through the synergistic actions of glucose deprivation and hydroxyl radical (•OH)-mediated oxidative damage. <sentence_start/>Critically, MPG(Fe) exhibited no tissue toxicity in uninfected mice. <sentence_start/>Our findings establish enzyme-mimetic nanozymes as a novel therapeutic platform against zoonotic helminthiases.
1. Introduction

Eosinophils, neutrophils, and monocytes (MONs) play key roles in the host resistance to parasite invasion and migration. <sentence_start/>Increased parasite killing correlates with elevated numbers of neutrophils and eosinophils, which possess surface peroxidases (PODs) with antiparasitic activity [<citation rid="bib-0001" ref-type="bibr" pmcid="PMC1541177" pmid="564249" count="1">1</citation>-<citation rid="bib-0003" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1365-3024.1981.tb00389.x" pmid="7243337" count="1">3</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In fact, H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> production catalyzed by eosinophil POD has been cited as evidence for an eosinophil/H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>/Cl<sup>−</sup> interaction mechanism, demonstrated to kill parasitic helminths in vitro [<citation rid="bib-0004" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/eji.1830111018" pmid="6273182" count="1">4</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Moreover, antibody-triggered neutrophil POD activity has been shown to kill helminths more effectively than eosinophil POD in vitro [<citation rid="bib-0005" ref-type="bibr" pmcid="PMC1454451" pmid="6321330" count="1">5</citation>].

Glucose oxidase (GOx), a natural enzyme approved for use in feed additives (as listed in China’s Catalog of Feed Additive Varieties), catalyzes the oxidation of endogenous glucose by oxygen, generating H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> and gluconic acid in situ [<citation rid="bib-0006" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fmicb.2022.994151" pmcid="PMC9578003" pmid="36267185" count="1">6</citation>, <citation rid="bib-0007" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/01652176.2024.2447592" pmcid="PMC11703519" pmid="39742888" count="1">7</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This reaction elevates local H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> concentrations, thereby enhancing the POD activity [<citation rid="bib-0008" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fphys.2021.646393" pmcid="PMC8244819" pmid="34220529" count="1">8</citation>]. <sentence_start/>POD-dependent oxidative reactions constitute a natural and effective antihelminthic defense mechanism. <sentence_start/>However, this mechanism relies on the recruitment and activation of host immune cells, which is delayed, energetically costly, and can be subverted by parasites. <sentence_start/>Therefore, we infer that a synthetic cascade reaction simulating the GOx/POD tandem is involved. <sentence_start/>In this reaction, GOx generates H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> in situ using the abundant glucose in the intestinal cavity, while the class POD nanoenzymes convert this H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> into more cytotoxic hydroxyl radicals (•OH). <sentence_start/>This strategy recreates and scales up the host’s natural oxidative killing in an in-cell manner and does not rely on the host’s immune status. <sentence_start/>Such systems hold significant promise for developing considerably more effective anti-helminthic therapies [<citation rid="bib-0009" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1039/D2TB02605H" pmid="36806466" count="1">9</citation>].

Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) have garnered significant attention in recent years owing to their distinctive properties, including high porosity, large surface area, tunable pore size, and compatibility with polymers, biomolecules, and metal nanoparticles [<citation rid="bib-0010" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/molecules25010168" pmcid="PMC6983047" pmid="31906165" count="1">10</citation>-<citation rid="bib-0013" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jcis.2024.05.211" pmid="38823114" count="1">13</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Notably, MOF-525(Fe) (hereafter referred to as MOF-Fe), which utilizes iron porphyrins as ligands, has been shown to exhibit high-level catalytic activity and thus has great potential as a nanomedicine [<citation rid="bib-0014" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/adfm.201910085" count="1">14</citation>-<citation rid="bib-0016" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1021/acsnano.1c04280" pmid="34160201" count="1">16</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The coordinated Fe atoms within its porphyrin groups confer POD-like activity, enabling the generation of H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, which can subsequently be converted into hydroxyl radicals (•OH) [<citation rid="bib-0016" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1021/acsnano.1c04280" pmid="34160201" count="1">16</citation>, <citation rid="bib-0017" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1021/acsnano.8b09501" pmid="31002497" count="1">17</citation>].

In enzymatic cascades, sequentially reacting enzymes often assemble into stable complexes to achieve efficient reaction pathways. <sentence_start/>However, simply mixing two distinct enzymes typically fails to form stable conjugates, resulting in significantly lower cascade activity compared to covalently linked enzyme systems [<citation rid="bib-0018" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1021/acs.nanolett.9b04959" pmid="31891508" count="1">18</citation>]. <sentence_start/>While enzymes can adsorb electrostatically onto MOF carriers, such attachments are often unstable under fluctuating pH and environmental conditions, leading to enzyme detachment [<citation rid="bib-0019" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1039/b506090g" count="1">19</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Enzyme reconstruction offers a solution to this instability, preventing enzyme leaching and enabling the continuous operation of multienzyme cascade systems. <sentence_start/>For instance, covalently conjugating enzymes to MOF-Fe can create robust cascade reaction systems exhibiting superior stability and resistance to environmental changes compared to systems utilizing freely diffusing enzymes [<citation rid="bib-0020" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1021/acscatal.8b04921" count="1">20</citation>].

The use of nanozymes for parasitic disease treatment offers an emerging strategy to circumvent chemical resistance development [<citation rid="bib-0021" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1021/acs.nanolett.9b03774" pmid="31671939" count="1">21</citation>]. <sentence_start/><italic>Trichinella spiralis</italic> is a typical zoonotic parasite that infect both humans and animals [<citation rid="bib-0022" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fcimb.2022.955974" pmcid="PMC9395740" pmid="36017365" count="1">22</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This pathogen colonizes intestinal and muscular tissues, posing severe threats to global food safety, livestock production, and regional economies, particularly in resource-limited settings [<citation rid="bib-0023" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.fm.2016.12.012" pmid="28213036" count="1">23</citation>, <citation rid="bib-0024" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3201/eid1712.110896" pmcid="PMC3311199" pmid="22172230" count="1">24</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Adult worm (AD) reside in the host’s small intestine, where they mate and release newborn larvae (NBL) that penetrate the intestinal barrier, enter the bloodstream, and ultimately muscle larval (ML) cysts in striated muscle for long-term survival [<citation rid="bib-0025" ref-type="bibr" count="1">25</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Crucially, the intestinal phase represents the most active period of <italic>T. spiralis</italic>’s life cycle, inducing severe host inflammatory responses [<citation rid="bib-0026" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.ppat.1003122" pmcid="PMC3547840" pmid="23349631" count="1">26</citation>, <citation rid="bib-0027" ref-type="bibr" count="1">27</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Therefore, <italic>T. spiralis</italic> is a highly representative model for intestinal parasitic infections [<citation rid="bib-0026" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.ppat.1003122" pmcid="PMC3547840" pmid="23349631" count="1">26</citation>, <citation rid="bib-0028" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1365-2184.2009.00605.x" pmcid="PMC3017958" pmid="19397593" count="1">28</citation>, <citation rid="bib-0029" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/gut.2006.118356" pmid="17675326" count="1">29</citation>].

Herein, we designed MPG(Fe), an integrated GOx/POD cascade system synthesized by conjugating GOx to a POD-like nanozyme, zirconium-based MOF-Fe, via a bifunctional PEG linker. <sentence_start/>Systematic pathogenicity assessment confirmed that MPG(Fe) significantly kills <italic>T. spiralis</italic>. <sentence_start/>This work pioneers a nanozyme-based antihelminthic therapeutic leveraging the GOx/POD cascade reaction, potentially enabling broader applications of nanozymes against zoonotic intestinal parasites.
2. Materials and Methods
2.1. Materials and Instrumentation

Zirconyl chloride octahydrate (ZrOCl<sub>2</sub>·8H<sub>2</sub>O, 99.9%), ferrous (II) chloride tetrahydrate (FeCl<sub>2</sub>·4H<sub>2</sub>O, 99.99%), N-hydroxy succinimide (NHS, 98%), N-(3-dimethylaminopropyl)-N′-ethylcarbodiimide hydrochloride (EDC·HCl, 98%), KBr (spectral grade), fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC, 95%), and 5,5-dimethyl-1-pyrroline N-oxide (DMPO, 97%) were purchased from Aladdin Ltd. (Shanghai). <sentence_start/>4,4<sup>′</sup>,4<sup>″</sup>,4<sup>‴</sup>-(porphine-5,10,15,20-tetrayl) tetrakis (benzoic acid) (TCPP, 97%) and methylene blue (98%) were purchased from TCI Development Co., Ltd. (Shanghai). <sentence_start/>2,2<sup>′</sup>-azinobis(3-ethylbenzothiazoline-6-sulfonic acid ammonium salt) (ABTS, 98%) and 3,3<sup>′</sup>,5,5<sup>′</sup>-tetramethylbenzidine (TMB, 99%) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich Ltd. Glucose (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub>, 99.5%) was purchased Amresco Ltd. Horseradish POD (HRP, ≥300 U mg<sup>−1</sup>) and GOx (100-250 U mg<sup>−1</sup>) were purchased from Shanghai Yuanye Bio-Technology Co., Ltd. High glucose Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium (DMEM), penicillin streptomycin (10,000 U mL<sup>−1</sup>), 3,5-dinitrosalicylic acid (DNS), 2-(N-morpholino)-ethane sulfonic acid (MES) and an Amino Acid Assay Kit were purchased from Beijing Solarbio Science & Technology Co., Ltd. Phosphate-buffered saline (PBS, pH 7.4, 1×) and a Bradford Protein Concentration Assay Kit were purchased from Sparkjade Science Co., Ltd. A Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8) was purchased from APExBIO Technology LLC. <sentence_start/>N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF, 99.5%), acetic acid (CH<sub>3</sub>COOH, 99.5%), hydrochloric acid (HCl, 36%), hydrogen peroxide solution (H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, 30%), and other chemicals and reagents were purchased from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd. Water was prepared using a Milli-Q water purification system that was purchased from Millipore.

Transmission electron microscope (TEM) images were taken using a JEOL JEM-2100F system operated using an accelerating voltage of 120 kV. <sentence_start/>Scanning electron microscope (SEM) images were obtained using a JEOL JSM-7900F SEM system. <sentence_start/>X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns were obtained using an R-AXIS RAPID system based on irradiation of samples with Cu Kα irradiation at a scan rate of 1° min<sup>−1</sup> using a target voltage of 40 kV and a current set to 40 mA. <sentence_start/>UV-vis absorption spectra were recorded using a UV-2700 UV-Vis spectrophotometer (Shimadzu, Japan). <sentence_start/>Analyses of Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectra were performed using a VERTEX 80V system (Brucker, Germany). <sentence_start/>Zeta potential data were analyzed using a Malvern NANO ZS90 instrument with a Ne laser (633 nm, 4 mW). <sentence_start/>Fluorescence microscopy images were obtained using an Olympus FV3000 confocal laser scanning microscope (CLSM).
2.2. <sentence_start/>Preparation of MOF-Fe, PEG-MOF-Fe (MP[Fe]), and GOx-MP(Fe) (MPG[Fe])

The TCPP-Fe was prepared by suspending 160 mg of TCPP and 400 mg of FeCl<sub>2</sub>·4H<sub>2</sub>O in 20 mL of DMF, followed by refluxing of the mixture at 200°C for 1 h. <sentence_start/>The solid material was washed three times with water and dried to generate a black solid. <sentence_start/>Next, MOF-525(Fe) (hereafter referred to as MOF-Fe) was synthesized according to Kelty’s procedure with slight modifications [<citation rid="bib-0030" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1039/C6CC03264H" pmid="27247981" count="1">30</citation>] and TCPP-Fe (94.9 mg) was dissolved in DMF (30 mL) in a 100-mL iodine flask using sonication. <sentence_start/>In the following step, acetic acid (0.2 mL) was added, and the resulting solution was heated to 90°C and then maintained at this temperature for 18 h. <sentence_start/>The resulting nanocrystal precipitates were collected by centrifugation (27,000 × <italic>g</italic>, 10 min) and then subjected to solvent exchange with DMF (3 × 10 mL). <sentence_start/>The resulting MOF-Fe solid was suspended in DMF for future use.

MOF was activated to remove unreacted organic ligands, metal salt ions, and solvent molecules present within the pores and surfaces of the material using a previously reported method [<citation rid="bib-0031" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/anie.201204475" pmid="22907870" count="1">31</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Briefly, MOF-Fe (30 mg) was dissolved in 20 mL of DMF using an ultrasound. <sentence_start/>Next, 0.75 mL of HCl (8 M) was added to the solution, and then the resulting solution was incubated at 120°C for 12 h to allow the reaction to proceed to completion. <sentence_start/>Crystals that formed were collected by centrifugation (27,000 × <italic>g</italic>, 10 min), and then solvent exchange with DMF was conducted (3 × 10 mL). <sentence_start/>The resulting MOF-Fe material was suspended in DMF for future use.

To synthesized PEG-MOF-Fe (MP[Fe]), the MOF-Fe was dissolved in 10 mL of DMF using ultrasound, then NH<sub>2</sub>─PEG─COOH (MW: 2000) was added to the solution at different mass ratios (PEG:MOF = 0.01:1, 0.05:1, 0.1:1, 0.25:1, 0.5:1, 1:1, 2:1, 4:1, and 8:1), and reactions were allowed to proceed to completion at 37°C for 6 h. <sentence_start/>Thereafter, precipitated material was collected by centrifugation (27,000 × <italic>g</italic>, 10 min) then subjected to solvent exchange with Milli-Q water (3 × 1 mL). <sentence_start/>Next, reaction products were placed in Labconco CentriVap Aqueous Concentrator Systems for use in evaporating the residual water. <sentence_start/>The efficiency of covalent conjugation of NH<sub>2</sub>─PEG─COOH to MOF-Fe in each reaction was determined using an Amino Acid Assay Kit (Beijing Solarbio Science & Technology Co., Ltd.).

GOx (10 mg) was dissolved in 2 mL of MES buffer (pH 6.5), then 100 μL of EDC (20 mM) was added to the tube, followed by gentle shaking of the tube at 37°C for 15 min. <sentence_start/>Subsequently, 100 μL of 20 mM NHS and 10 mL of MP(Fe) (1 mg mL<sup>−1</sup>) were added to the abovementioned solution, followed by incubation of the resulting solution for 1 h at 37°C. <sentence_start/>Finally, MPG(Fe) was obtained by centrifugation (15000 rpm, 10 min) followed by solvent exchange with Milli-Q water (3 × 1 mL). <sentence_start/>Thereafter, the final GOx-MP(Fe) (MPG[Fe]) preparation was placed in a Labconco CentriVap Aqueous Concentrator System to remove residual Milli-Q water via evaporation. <sentence_start/>The efficiency of covalent conjugation of GOx to MP(Fe) was determined using a Bradford Protein Concentration Assay Kit (Sparkjade Biotechnology Co., Ltd.).
2.3. POD Mimetic Activities of MOF-Fe and MPG(Fe)

Km and Vmax values associated with MOF-Fe POD mimetic activity were calculated using a Lineweaver-Burk plot by surveying initial rates of reactions containing various H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> concentrations (ranging from 0.01 to 25.0 mM) in the presence of 2 mM TMB or various TMB concentrations (ranging from 0.0625 to 4.0 mM) in the presence of 25 mM H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>. <sentence_start/>The POD mimetic activity of MPG(Fe) was measured by monitoring ABTS absorbance intensity changes in the presence of MPG(Fe) and H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> through the analysis of UV/vis spectra collected at 417 nm. <sentence_start/>The effect of pH on MPG(Fe) POD mimetic activity was studied within the pH range of 2.0-12.0. <sentence_start/>The effect of temperature on MPG(Fe) POD-mimetic activity was investigated within the temperature range of 15-45°C. <sentence_start/>Meanwhile, different concentrations of MPG(Fe) (0, 20, or 50 μg mL<sup>−1</sup>) were added into 20 mL of PBS buffer (initial pH 7.4) containing 50 mg mL<sup>−1</sup> glucose, and then pH value measurements were taken using a real-time pH meter.
2.4. •OH Generation Ability of MPG(Fe)

DMPO served as a trapping probe for use in electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopic monitoring of •OH generation ([H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>] = 100 μM, [MPG(Fe)] = 100 μg mL<sup>−1</sup>). <sentence_start/>In addition, •OH generation was monitored via fluorescence spectroscopy, a method based on terephthalic acid (TA) capture of •OH that generates a 2-hydroxy TA product that uniquely fluoresces when excited with light of wavelength approximately 435 nm. <sentence_start/>Briefly, HAc-NaAc buffer solutions (pH 6.0, 10 mM) containing TA (0.5 mM), H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> (1 mM), and/or MOF-Fe (100 μg mL<sup>−1</sup>) were prepared, and then reaction tubes containing TA, TA with H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, TA with MOF-Fe, and TA with MOF-Fe and H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> were prepared. <sentence_start/>Reactions were allowed to proceed for 12 h, and then reaction tubes were centrifuged. <sentence_start/>Thereafter, the fluorescence spectra of the resulting supernatants were obtained and analyzed.
2.5. Glucose Consumption

MPG(Fe) solutions at different concentrations (50, 100, and 200 μg mL<sup>−1</sup>) were added to a 1 mg mL<sup>−1</sup> glucose solution, and then the DNS method was used to monitor the glucose concentration during the reaction. <sentence_start/>In brief, at different time points, 0.2 mL aliquots of the abovementioned solutions were removed and centrifuged. <sentence_start/>Next, 0.8 mL of DNS was added to each sample, and then tubes containing samples were heated at 100°C for 5 min, quickly cooled in a water bath and left there for 20 min. <sentence_start/>Absorbance intensity changes were monitored via UV/vis spectroscopy conducted at 540 nm.
2.6. H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> Generation

H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> generation was assessed by conducting ABTS UV-vis absorbance measurements at 734 nm in the presence of HRP (HRP). <sentence_start/>In brief, first glucose (50 mg mL<sup>−1</sup>) and MPG(Fe) (50, 100, and 200 μg mL<sup>−1</sup>) were mixed. <sentence_start/>Next, 200 μL aliquots of the solution were removed at different time points, then 50 μL of HRP (1 U mL<sup>−1</sup>), 850 μL of HAc-NaAc buffer (pH 6.0, 10 mM), and 100 μL of ABTS (2 mM) were added to each aliquot. <sentence_start/>After reactions proceeded for 10 min, ABTS absorbance intensity changes of reactions were monitored by recording UV/vis spectra at 734 nm in order to quantify the sample H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> concentrations based on a standard curve generated using the same method.
2.7. <sentence_start/><italic>In Vitro</italic> Cytotoxicity of MOF-Fe and MPG(Fe)

IPEC-J2 cells were used for in vitro experiments. <sentence_start/>Cells were maintained in high glucose DMEM containing 10% fetal bovine serum and 1% penicillin streptomycin (10,000 U mL<sup>−1</sup>) in an atmosphere of 5% CO<sub>2</sub> at 37°C.

IPEC-J2 cells (5 × 10<sup>3</sup> cells well<sup>−1</sup>) were cultured in 96 well plates (Jet Bio-Filtration Co., Ltd.) for 24 h at 37°C. <sentence_start/>Next, MOF-Fe or MPG(Fe) was added to wells of plates to achieve final concentrations of 1.5, 3, 6, 12, 25, 50, or 100 μg mL<sup>−1</sup>. <sentence_start/>Thereafter, plates were incubated for an additional 6, 12, or 24 h, and then cell viability was assessed using the CCK 8 method.
2.8. <sentence_start/>Ethical Treatment of Animals and <italic>T. spiralis</italic> Organisms

In this study, 6- to 8-week-old male Wistar rats weighing approximately 200 g and 6- to 8-week-old male BALB/c mice weighing approximately 20 g were used in experiments. <sentence_start/>Animals were fed normal chow and distilled water and housed in an animal room where the temperature was maintained at 24 ± 2°C, humidity at 55% ± 5% and lighting set to a 12 h day/12 h night cycle. <sentence_start/>All animal experiments were performed according to regulations of the Administration of Affairs Concerning Experimental Animals in China using protocols that were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of Jilin University (No. SY202511035). <sentence_start/><italic>T. spiralis</italic> (ISS534) parasites were provided by the Institute of Zoonosis, Jilin University.
2.9. <sentence_start/>Preparation of <italic>T. spiralis</italic> Adult (AD) Worms

ADs were collected according to the method previously studied from small intestines of 8- to 10-week-old Wistar rats that had been inoculated 3 days earlier with 5000 larvae [<citation rid="bib-0032" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pntd.0011479" pmcid="PMC10431649" pmid="37585413" count="1">32</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Briefly, intestines were washed, then intestinal samples were suspended in saline containing 2× penicillin-streptomycin, and then, samples were incubated at 37°C for 2 h. <sentence_start/>Thereafter, the small intestine tissue fragments and the upper layer of liquid were carefully removed, and then the remaining liquid containing ADs was transferred to a flat dish. <sentence_start/>Next, ADs were rinsed repeatedly with saline to remove small intestine debris. <sentence_start/>Next, washed ADs were resuspended and cultured in RMPI 1640 medium containing 2× penicillin-streptomycin until needed for experiments.
2.10. <sentence_start/>Preparation of NBL

After 8- to 10-week-old Wistar rats were inoculated with 5000 larvae, ADs were collected from small intestines of rats 5 days later using the abovementioned procedure. <sentence_start/>Thereafter, collected ADs were cultured in RMPI 1640 medium containing 2× penicillin-streptomycin and 10% FBS at 37°C in 5% CO<sub>2</sub> for 24 h. <sentence_start/>NBLs were separated from ADs via filtration using a Falcon Cell Strainer (100 μm hole size) and incubated in RMPI 1640 medium (containing 2× penicillin-streptomycin) until subjected to further analysis.
2.11. <sentence_start/>Effects of MPG(Fe) Treatment on ADs and NBLs <italic>In Vitro</italic>

ADs (10 to 20 worms well<sup>−1</sup>) were cultured in 12 well plates (Jet Bio-Filtration Co., Ltd.) and NBLs (30 to 40 larvae per well) were cultured in 96 well plates (Jet Bio-Filtration Co., Ltd.). <sentence_start/>ADs were cultured in PBS or MPG(Fe) at different concentrations (5, 10, 25, 50, or 100 μg mL<sup>−1</sup>) in wells of 12 well plates in a total volume/well of 2 mL of PBS (pH 7.4) containing 5% glucose. <sentence_start/>For NBLs, larvae in wells of 96-well plates were treated with PBS or MPG(Fe) at different concentrations (5, 10, 50, or 100 μg mL<sup>−1</sup>) in a total volume/well of 0.2 mL of PBS (pH 7.4) containing 5% glucose. <sentence_start/>Numbers of viable and dead ADs and NBLs in tissues were determined by viewing Hoechst- and propidium iodide (PI)-stained tissues under a CLSM. <sentence_start/>In addition, numbers of ADs were determined to assess the effects of free GOx and MOF-Fe exposures on AD viability.
2.12. <sentence_start/>Effects of MPG(Fe) Treatment on ADs <italic>In Vivo</italic>

BALB/c mice (aged 6-8 weeks) were inoculated with 500 larvae and injected intraperitoneally with low-dose (2.5 mg kg<sup>−1</sup>), medium-dose (7.5 mg kg<sup>−1</sup>), high-dose (15 mg kg<sup>−1</sup>) MPG(Fe), or PBS at 6, 12, and 24 h after larval inoculation. <sentence_start/>At 30-h after inoculation, ADs were collected using the abovementioned method, and then dead larvae were counted.
2.13. <sentence_start/>Evaluation of MPG(Fe) Biosafety and Toxicity <italic>In Vivo</italic>

To evaluate MPG(Fe) therapeutic safety and toxicity, 6- to 8-week-old BALB/c mice were randomly assigned to two groups for short-term (6, 12, 24, and 30 h) and long-term (1, 3, 5, and 7 days) MPG(Fe) administration. <sentence_start/>Subgroups of mice within the two groups were treated with PBS or low-dose MPG(Fe) (2.5 mg kg<sup>−1</sup>), medium-dose MPG(Fe) (7.5 mg kg<sup>−1</sup>) or high-dose MPG(Fe) (15 mg kg<sup>−1</sup>). <sentence_start/>All animal studies were performed according to protocols that were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of Jilin University.
2.14. <sentence_start/>Blood Biochemical Index Analysis

Blood samples were collected from eye orbital veins of mice in both groups using 1 mL blood collection microtubes containing ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) anticoagulant. <sentence_start/>White blood cells (WBCs), lymph (lymphocyte), MONs, neutrophilic granulocyte (Gran), neutrophilic Gran%, red blood cells (RBCs), hemoglobin (HGB), and blood platelet (PLT) values were obtained for each blood sample using a Mindray BC-2800vet Veterinary Automated Hematology Analyzer.
2.15. <sentence_start/>Flow Cytometric Analysis of Mouse Splenic T and B Cells

Spleens were excised from mice of the two groups, then spleens were pulverized and filtered (100-mesh) and spleen cells were resuspended in PBS. <sentence_start/>RBCs were removed after spleen cells were centrifuged at 260 × <italic>g</italic> for 10 min by discarding the pellet and then resuspending nonpelleted cells in Red Blood Cell Lysis Buffer (Solarbio) to lyse residual RBCs. <sentence_start/>The remaining intact cells were washed 2-3 times with PBS and then adjusted to a cell count per volume of 5 × 10<sup>6</sup> cells mL<sup>−1</sup>. <sentence_start/>Suspended T and B cells were prepared for flow cytometric analysis by incubating them with a phycoerythrin (PE)-conjugated antibody that specifically binds to the CD45 leukocyte marker present on all hematopoietic cells except PLTs and erythrocytes (BioLegend 103105), an allophycocyanin (APC)-conjugated antibody that specifically binds to the CD45R marker found on surfaces of B cells and subsets of T cells and NK cells (BioLegend 103211) or a FITC-conjugated antibody that specifically binds to the T cell receptor component CD3e present on T cell surfaces (BD Pharmingen 553061). <sentence_start/>After cells were incubated with the abovementioned antibodies, they were washed with PBS, and then 10<sup>6</sup> cells from each sample were analyzed using a BDverse flow cytometer. <sentence_start/>All data sets were analyzed using FlowJo 10 data analysis software (FLOWJO, LLC).
2.16. <sentence_start/>Immunofluorescence Staining

4. Discussion

Nanozymes leverage exceptional physicochemical properties, low cost, and high stability to overcome limitations inherent in natural enzymes [<citation rid="bib-0039" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/adma.202211210" pmid="36840985" count="1">39</citation>, <citation rid="bib-0040" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1021/acs.chemrev.8b00672" pmid="30801188" count="1">40</citation>]. <sentence_start/>These synthetic enzymes have demonstrated therapeutic efficacy against diverse pathologies, including tumors, bacterial infections and inflammatory disorders [<citation rid="bib-0041" ref-type="bibr" pmcid="PMC8167679" pmid="34094660" count="1">41</citation>-<citation rid="bib-0044" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/adma.202409840" pmid="39690880" count="1">44</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Here, we report MPG(Fe), a hybrid cascade system integrating natural GOx with a POD-mimetic nanozyme. <sentence_start/>This platform represents a novel strategy for treating trichinellosis and other zoonotic intestinal parasitic diseases.

During the <italic>T. spiralis</italic> life cycle, it dynamically shifts energy sources across developmental stages and infection sites (intestinal and muscle tissue). <sentence_start/>Upon entering the intestinal environment, ML rapidly initiate growth and development, fueled primarily by endogenous glycogen reserves synthesized in prior parasitized tissues [<citation rid="bib-0045" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/0020-7519(86)90079-2" pmid="2430908" count="1">45</citation>, <citation rid="bib-0046" ref-type="bibr" count="1">46</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Critically, intestinal adults face rapid mortality once these glycogen stores deplete unless they absorb substantial exogenous glucose to sustain energy demands. <sentence_start/>This glucose dependence is evidenced by in vitro studies, adult worms perish within 12 h without exogenous glucose [<citation rid="bib-0038" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1017/S0031182000081282" pmid="3797065" count="1">38</citation>], confirming glucose as essential for parasitism and development.

MOF-Fe comprises octahedral Zr<sub>6</sub> clusters capped by eight <italic>μ<sub>3</sub> </italic>-OH ligands. <sentence_start/>Four of the 12 cluster edges coordinate TCPP-Fe linkers (5,10,15,20-tetrakis-(4-carboxyphenyl)-porphyrin-Fe chloride), while the remaining Zr sites bind 16 terminals ─OH ligands [<citation rid="bib-0031" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/anie.201204475" pmid="22907870" count="1">31</citation>, <citation rid="bib-0036" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1021/ic300825s" pmid="22676251" count="1">36</citation>, <citation rid="bib-0047" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1021/ja4050828" pmid="23829224" count="1">47</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This architecture confers exceptional POD-like activity through two synergistic features: (1) iron porphyrin catalytic centers and (2) unsaturated Zr<sub>6</sub> sites, enabling functionalization. <sentence_start/>Within MPG(Fe), PEG covalently conjugates MOF-Fe to GOx, creating a dual-enzyme system with superior antiparasitic activity compared to either enzyme alone. <sentence_start/>PEG plays a triple synergistic role in this coupling strategy. <sentence_start/>First, as a chemical linker, its carboxyl terminus is covalently connected to the unsaturated Zr<sub>6</sub> site of MOF-Fe through a solvent-assisted ligand incorporation method, while its amino terminus is coupled to the carboxyl group of GOx through EDC/NHS chemistry, thereby forming a stable GOx-PEG-MOF(Fe) covalent complex. <sentence_start/>Second, as a flexible spacer arm, it can reduce the spatial steric hindrance between the enzyme and the MOF surface and maintain the catalytic activity of GOx. <sentence_start/>Finally, as a hydrophilic anti-fouling layer, it can significantly improve the water solubility and colloidal dispersion of the complex and prevent the particles from aggregating in the electrolyte-containing biological medium. <sentence_start/>Stability assays confirmed that covalent PEG conjugation significantly enhances MPG(Fe) robustness over electrostatically adsorbed GOx. <sentence_start/>This design enables a unique GOx/POD cascade effect, positioning MPG(Fe) as a potent chemotherapeutic agent.

Mechanistically, MOF-Fe provides POD-mimetic activity via its iron-porphyrin centers, while GOx activity was not affected by the structure. <sentence_start/>Within the intestinal microenvironment, GOx in MPG(Fe) depletes local glucose via conversion to gluconic acid and H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, critically restricting nutrient acquisition by <italic>T. spiralis</italic>. <sentence_start/>Concomitantly, the generated H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> fuels MPG(Fe)’s POD-mimetic activity, accelerating •OH radical production, inducing lethal oxidative stress in <italic>T. spiralis</italic>. <sentence_start/>It is also worth noting that the GOx-catalyzed production of gluconic acid gradually acidifies the local microenvironment. <sentence_start/>This acidification may promote parasite killing through two mechanisms. <sentence_start/>First, it directly disrupts the physiological activities of the intestinal <italic>T. spiralis</italic> that has adapted to the mildly alkaline intestinal environment, while enhancing the POD mimetic activity of the MOF-Fe component, thereby accelerating the production of •OH. <sentence_start/>These two effects have a synergistic effect. <sentence_start/>The reduction of glucose consumption lowers the pH, thereby accelerating the conversion of the co-generated H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> into cytotoxic •OH. <sentence_start/>In the body, this acidification is expected to be localized, and most of it will be buffered by the intestinal contents.

The very rapid killing of NBLs is faster than would be expected from oxidative damage alone and warrants consideration of an additional physical component. <sentence_start/>The granular substances visible in the processed larval images are likely to represent aggregated MPG(Fe) nanoparticles, which may adhere to the surface of the larvae. <sentence_start/>It is therefore plausible that direct nanoparticle-membrane contact contributes to membrane rupture and accelerates killing, in addition to the chemical effects. <sentence_start/>Two observations support a predominantly chemical, concentration-dependent mechanism rather than a purely mechanical rupture. <sentence_start/>First, killing was strongly dose- and time-dependent, which is characteristic of a catalytic/oxidative process. <sentence_start/>Second, MOF-Fe alone, at the same particle concentrations, exerted no antiparasitic effect, indicating that mere particle contact without the GOx/POD cascade does not kill the worms. <sentence_start/>Nevertheless, we cannot fully exclude a mechanical contribution, and we have added this as an explicit limitation. <sentence_start/>The current first-line treatment drug for trichinellosis is albendazole. <sentence_start/>Its advantages include being approved for the market, having a low cost, being orally administered, and having certain activity against migrating and encysted muscle larvae. <sentence_start/>However, it has poor water solubility and low oral bioavailability; and there are risks of liver toxicity, bone marrow suppression, and the possibility of developing drug resistance in veterinary use. <sentence_start/>MPG(Fe) does not target the microtubule polymerization pathway of the parasite but instead kills intestinal-stage parasites through a dual, self-amplifying mechanism, which may avoid cross-resistance to existing drugs. <sentence_start/>In terms of biosafety, although no detectable acute toxicity was observed in the mice during the test period, it should be emphasized that the biosafety data presented in this study are solely derived from uninfected healthy mice and the observation period is short. <sentence_start/>Since <italic>T. spiralis</italic> infection itself induces intestinal barrier disruption and mucosal inflammation, this may alter the absorption, clearance, and toxicity characteristics of MPG(Fe). <sentence_start/>Therefore, the results of this study cannot be directly extrapolated to infected individuals, and the safety and long-term toxicity of MPG(Fe) in infected hosts still need to be determined through future research.
5. Conclusions

This study provides a proof-of-concept that a covalently conjugated GOx/POD-mimetic cascade nanozyme (MPG[Fe]) can kill intestinal-stage <italic>T. spiralis</italic> in vitro and markedly reduce adult-worm burden in a mouse model through the combined actions of glucose starvation and •OH-mediated oxidative damage. <sentence_start/>These findings support the further exploration of enzyme-mimetic nanomaterials as an alternative mechanistic strategy against intestinal helminthiases.
